newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland has room for higher rates - c. bank adviser.
newsitem.headline: Poland has room for higher rates - c. bank adviser.

text.p: Poland's central bank sees room for more monetary tightening but believes that only combining this with a tighter budget can cool booming demand and control a gaping trade deficit, a senior adviser to the bank said.

"The NBP (National Bank of Poland) is aware that certain further monetary tightening is probably necessary and possible but the NBP is not certain it (alone) will be effective," Stanislaw Gomulka told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday.
"That is why the bank is demanding fiscal adjustments which it knows would be effective," he added.

Gomulka said that because Polish companies, individuals and local governments were catching up with borrowing after several years of debt-free financing such a powerful trend could prove hard to control for the next few years -- before the economy reaches sufficient saturation levels.

"I expect that this wave of rising credit will eventually end, but now the total debt of the non-government sector amounts to 20-25 percent of GDP (gross domestic product) and it can easily reach 50 percent in the next few years," Gomulka said.

He said that because the natural pressure on credit growth was so strong monetary tightening might have limited impact on non-government borrowers and in order to cap total credit and demand government borrowing has to be slashed.

The finance ministry plans to cut the budget deficit to 1.9 percent of gross domestic product next year from the 2.8 percent 1997 plan, but the central bank has said this reduction was not deep enough to cool buoyant demand.
Gomulka reiterated the NBP stance that it saw next year's deficit of 1.5 percent as the highest acceptable level provided a balanced budget was be reached in 1999.
"Ideally the NBP would like to see a balanced budget in 1998 and even a surplus in 1999," he said.
The bank has warned that a 1.9 percent budget gap next year could result in the trade deficit growing to $16 billion or 7-8 percent of GDP from $12 billion or 5-6 percent expected in 1997.

Gomulka said that uncertainty over Poland's external position and the resulting bearish zloty sentiment made it possible for the central bank to raise interest rates without luring massive inflows of speculative foreign capital.

"We do not see pressure from foreign capital. I do not know what would happen if interest rates rose by five points but I believe there is a room for manoeuvre and rates could go up by 2-3 points," he said.

The central bank has kept its lombard and discount rates unchanged for a year at 25 and 22 percent respectively, allowing real rates to rise along with falling inflation which slipped to 14.6 percent year-on-year in May.
The NBP has also upped mandatory reserve requirements twice this year and earlier this week propped up its main market drainage rate by nearly half a point to 22.59 percent.
But Gomulka said the NBP was concerned that further monetary tightening would make Polish companies seek foreign credit using domestic banks as intermediaries.
"I do not know how Polish banks, firms and local governments will react to a rise in interest rates and whether they will not start taking foreign credits," he said.

Gomulka said that now Western institutions were still cautious about lending to Polish banks and corporations but Poland's overall success story could soon trigger a stream of foreign lending to the non-government sector.
